title: {{NAME}} and the Night the Fireflies Answered
moral: The smallest creatures carry the brightest magic when someone takes the time to listen.

pages.content:
The meadow behind the old stone wall was the kind of place most people walked past without looking, which was precisely why it was extraordinary. {{NAME}} had found it by following a hedgehog, which is generally an excellent way to discover things worth discovering. The hedgehog had waddled through a gap in the mossy stones and vanished, and {{NAME}} had squeezed through after it into a meadow that shimmered with its own quiet light.

The grass was knee-high and silver-tipped, though no moon had risen yet. Wildflowers nodded in colours he had no names for. And threading between every stem, every petal, every dewdrop, were lights. Dozens of them. Hundreds. Moving with unmistakable purpose and laughing in voices that sounded like water over small stones.

The hedgehog sat in the middle of it all as though it had been expecting this, its small eyes dark and knowing. {{NAME}} stood at the meadow's edge and stared with his whole heart.

pages.content:
One of the lights flew directly up to {{NAME}}'s nose and stopped. It was a fairy, but not the kind from paintings. She was small as his thumb and intensely serious, with wings like a dragonfly's and a coat sewn from a single folded oak leaf. Her name was Fenn, and she crossed her arms and looked at {{NAME}} as though she was deciding something important.

'You followed Bramble,' she said, pointing at the hedgehog, who had not moved. 'Bramble only leads people who are ready.'

{{NAME}}'s eyebrows went up. His mouth opened and then closed again. A dozen other fairies had gathered in a hovering semicircle behind Fenn, all of them watching him with bright, curious, relentless eyes.

'Ready for what?' {{NAME}} managed at last.

Fenn's serious expression cracked open into a grin that lit up the whole meadow. 'For the finding, obviously,' she said.

pages.content:
The finding, it turned out, was urgent. A young barn owl named Sable had lost her voice to an enchanted fog that rolled in on still nights and stole sounds it wanted to keep. Without her call, Sable could not find her way home across the dark fields, and her family had been circling above the meadow for three nights, calling out but hearing nothing back.

Fenn led the charge with {{NAME}} running full tilt behind her, barefoot through the cool grass, Bramble the hedgehog somehow keeping pace despite having legs barely longer than pencils. The fairy squadron scattered across the meadow in a coordinated sweep, each one calling out to the fog in the old language, which sounded to {{NAME}} like bells rolling down a hillside.

Sable perched on a low branch at the meadow's far end, her amber eyes enormous, her beak opening and closing in silent distress. {{NAME}} reached her first, climbing the fence post beside her, and cupped her gently in both hands, his warmth flowing into her cold feathers.

pages.content:
The enchanted fog pressed in from all sides, cold and hungry, swirling around the fence post in thick coils. It did not like being challenged. It pulled at Fenn's wings, dimmed the other fairies, and made the meadow go very dark and very quiet in the way that feels like holding your breath.

{{NAME}} kept both hands cupped around Sable, steady and sure. He could feel the owl's tiny heartbeat against his palms, quick as a ticking watch but not quite as terrified as before.

Fenn landed on {{NAME}}'s shoulder. She pressed one small hand against his cheek and looked at him with absolute conviction. Then she turned to the fog and sang. It was one note, perfectly held, and every other fairy found it and added their voices until the meadow rang like a glass bowl struck just right. The fog recoiled. It shivered. It unwound.

From Sable's open beak came one small, clear, perfect hoot. Then another. From high above, three answering calls dropped down through the dark like falling stars.

pages.content:
Sable's family descended in a soft rush of wings and gathered around her on the fence rail, three owls pressing close and hooting quietly to one another. Bramble sat below them looking satisfied in the way only hedgehogs can, which is completely and without any fuss at all.

Fenn settled on {{NAME}}'s shoulder again and this time did not say anything. She just sat there, swinging her small legs, while the meadow filled back up with its quiet silver light and the fairy squadron began drifting lazily through the flowers again.

{{NAME}} sat down in the cool grass and Bramble immediately climbed onto his foot, which was not comfortable but which {{NAME}} did not move to change. The stars above were extraordinary. The meadow hummed. Sable gave him one slow, amber-eyed blink before tucking her head under her wing.

His eyes grew heavy, then heavier. Tomorrow the meadow would be full of new mysteries, and Fenn had already hinted, very casually, that the fog never gave back what it took without a good reason. Goodnight, dear finder. The meadow will keep its secrets safe until morning.
